clue.text: Pure love? Cold as cold can be

parts.note: pure in the sense of utter or complete, as in pure nonsense
love is nil in tennis scoring, so a nought

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether pure love can be utterly cold.
explanation.definitionFit: The lowest temperature physically possible, about minus 273 degrees Celsius, where nothing could be chillier.

clue.text: Gets together a huge Donkey Derby field

explanation.surface: A crowd gathers for a donkey race with a very large field of runners.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is a pun: a huge field of donkeys is 'a mass (of) asses'. A Donkey Derby is a British fun race run on donkeys at fetes.
explanation.definitionFit: To collect or accumulate is to gather things together; the pun reads the word as a crowd of donkeys.

clue.text: Close formation at end of column

indicators.note: a formation is an arrangement, so the letters of the word close are formed anew

explanation.surface: Troops in close formation are drawn up at the end of a column.
explanation.definitionFit: A plinth or low block on which a column or pedestal rests, its lowest end.

clue.text: Ludicrous as Joyce's nickname

explanation.surface: Someone mocks a woman called Joyce for her silly nickname.
explanation.walkthrough: William Joyce, the wartime Nazi broadcaster, was nicknamed Lord Haw-Haw; 'haw-haw' is a laugh, so his nickname was laughter-worthy.
explanation.definitionFit: Absurd, ridiculous; the second sense puns on Lord Haw-Haw, a name made of a guffaw.

clue.text: Would-be expert must put time in to become one

definitions.text: Would-be expert must put time in to become one

parts.words: Would-be expert must put time in to become one
parts.note: a learner hoping to master a skill has to spend hours practising before becoming a master

explanation.surface: Advice that anyone wanting mastery must log the hours first.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue describes a beginner, who aspires to expertise; a learner must put time in to become an expert, and one is also what the beginner is.
explanation.definitionFit: A novice or beginner is someone starting out and hoping to become skilled.

clue.text: Such heavenly twins!

parts.note: the heavenly twins are Castor and Pollux, the constellation Gemini, one of the star signs

explanation.surface: An exclamation admiring a pair of delightful twins.
explanation.definitionFit: Relating to the band of twelve star signs, of which Gemini, the Twins, is one.

clue.text: This merrymaking overturned the bar

indicators.note: overturned means the word for a bar is turned round and read backwards

parts.note: a lever is a bar used to prise or lift

explanation.surface: Rowdy celebrations ended with the pub bar knocked over.
explanation.definitionFit: Lively festivity or partying, synonym for boisterous celebration.

clue.text: Two-masted vessel helps, we hear, army units

parts.note: a brig is a square-rigged sailing ship with two masts

indicators.note: we hear signals that the word for helps is taken by its sound only

parts.note: aids means helps

explanation.surface: A two-masted ship apparently assists some army units.
explanation.definitionFit: Large military formations, each made up of several battalions.

clue.text: Miller was a fool

explanation.surface: A statement that someone named Miller was foolish.
explanation.walkthrough: Joe Miller was an 18th-century English comic actor whose name was put on a famous joke book.
explanation.definitionFit: A professional clown or court joker; Joe Miller was a comedian whose name became a byword for old jokes.

clue.text: Equipped with a small volume, not in colour

parts.note: cc, cubic centimetres, is a small measure of volume
out is the opposite of in
red is a colour

explanation.surface: Someone was kitted out with a slim book, not in colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Dressed or fitted out with the gear needed, an old-fashioned synonym.

clue.text: Milton's harmonious (but non-vocal) sister

parts.note: in Milton's poem At a Solemn Music the 'harmonious sisters' are Voice and her sibling, poetry, the one that is not voice

explanation.surface: A description of a sister of Milton who was musical but did not sing.
explanation.walkthrough: Milton's ode At a Solemn Music opens 'Blest pair of Sirens, pledges of Heaven's joy, Sphere-born harmonious sisters, Voice and Verse'.
explanation.definitionFit: Poetry, metrical writing, which Milton paired with Voice as harmonious sisters.

clue.text: Look at the bubble!

parts.note: to look at something is to see it
taken as written

explanation.surface: An instruction to watch the bubble forming.
explanation.definitionFit: To boil or foam with bubbles, as a liquid does when heated.

clue.text: What will the sky do at dawn to make this unnecessary?

definitions.text: What will the sky do at dawn to make this unnecessary?

parts.words: What will the sky do at dawn to make this unnecessary?
parts.note: at dawn the sky grows bright, so a candle is no longer needed; the clue asks what the sky does

explanation.surface: A question about why some lamp is not needed once day breaks.
explanation.walkthrough: The sky will 'wax light' (grow bright) at dawn, and then a wax candle is unnecessary.
explanation.definitionFit: A taper or candle made of wax, made redundant by daylight.

clue.text: What's said to be left of this artist's pencils?

definitions.text: What's said to be left of this artist's pencils?

parts.words: What's said to be left of this artist's pencils?
parts.note: worn-down pencils leave short ends behind, and the painter's name is pronounced like those ends

explanation.surface: A question about the remnants of a painter's drawing pencils.
explanation.walkthrough: George Stubbs was an 18th-century English painter famous for horses; his name sounds like the stubs of used pencils.
explanation.definitionFit: George Stubbs, English painter of horses, whose surname sounds like worn pencil ends.

clue.text: Omnipresence of jumble I buy without leave

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the jumbled letters go around the word for leave
a jumble is a muddle, so the letters of I buy are mixed up

parts.note: to quit is to leave

explanation.surface: Something is everywhere because of a jumble sale purchase made without permission.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' means outside: UBIY (the anagram of I BUY, from 'jumble of') goes around QUIT.
explanation.definitionFit: The state of being everywhere at once, a synonym for being present in all places.

clue.text: About one who lent (his horse to John Gilpin)

parts.note: ca, short for circa, means about
a lender is someone who lends

explanation.surface: A story about someone who loaned a horse to John Gilpin.
explanation.walkthrough: In Cowper's comic ballad John Gilpin, the hero rides a horse borrowed from his friend the calender (a cloth-presser), and the clue's definition runs on from 'one who lent'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Cowper's poem the horse belongs to a calender, a man who presses cloth, Gilpin's friend.

clue.text: It's manifested mysteriously, in Tom's place

indicators.note: mysteriously suggests the words Tom's place are scrambled in some strange fashion

parts.note: taken with its s as written

explanation.surface: Something appears in a spooky way inside Tom's house.
explanation.definitionFit: The ghostly substance spiritualist mediums claimed to produce, materialising at seances.

clue.text: Fish etc with small anchor on endless reel

parts.note: a kedge is a small anchor used for warping a ship

indicators.note: endless says the word reel loses its final letter

explanation.surface: Fishing tackle: a small anchor attached to a reel with no end of line.
explanation.definitionFit: An Anglo-Indian dish of flaked fish, rice and eggs, hence fish and other things.

clue.text: I've little evidence about how timber was damaged

indicators.note: about means the scrap of evidence goes around the other piece

parts.note: a shred is a tiny scrap, as in not a shred of evidence
taken as written, the apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A detective admits to having little proof of how the wood was spoiled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shiver my timbers' is the stock pirate oath; to shiver is to shatter into splinters.
explanation.definitionFit: To shatter into fragments, as in the sailor's oath about timbers.

clue.text: Provide in no unbending fashion

explanation.surface: An instruction to deliver goods flexibly.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense reads the word as 'supple-y': in a supple way, not unbending.
explanation.definitionFit: To furnish or give; also, punningly, in a lithe or flexible manner.

clue.text: Assist resolution of circulation problem

indicators.note: resolution in the sense of breaking up into parts, so the letters of assist are reassembled

explanation.surface: Someone helps solve a blood-flow problem.
explanation.definitionFit: In medicine, a stoppage in the flow of blood or other body fluid.

clue.text: Moved to ecstasy about unusual gem's cut

indicators.note: about shows the word for thrilled surrounds the rest

parts.note: sent means thrilled or transported, as in music that sends you

indicators.note: unusual signals that the letters of the word gem are put in an odd order

parts.note: the possessive s is not counted

explanation.surface: A jeweller is thrilled by the cut of an unusual stone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts MEG (the anagram of GEM, from 'unusual') inside SENT.
explanation.definitionFit: A section or piece separated off from a whole, such as a slice of an orange.

clue.text: What P.O. charges for the same

definitions.text: What P.O. charges for the same

parts.words: What P.O. charges for the same
parts.note: a Post Office levies a fee on each postal order, reckoned per unit of sterling, and the order itself is a P.O. too

explanation.surface: A question about the fee a post office charges.
explanation.walkthrough: P.O. is both Post Office and postal order, so 'the same' is a postal order bought at the Post Office; the fee charged per pound sterling is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A charge or commission levied at a fixed rate per pound, as on postal orders.

clue.text: Split money for repair of drain

indicators.note: repair means the letters of the word drain are put back together in new working order

explanation.surface: Someone needs to spend money to mend a broken drain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Split' is not about dividing: it is the Croatian city, once in Yugoslavia, whose currency was this.
explanation.definitionFit: The currency unit of former Yugoslavia, used in the city of Split.

clue.text: Well bound

explanation.surface: Two words: fine, and leap.
explanation.definitionFit: A natural source of water from the ground, and a leap or jump.

clue.text: Make deduction in material for French railway

parts.note: taken as written
fer is French for iron, the metal of the chemin de fer, the French railway

explanation.surface: Someone works out what material is used in a French railway.
explanation.definitionFit: To deduce or conclude by reasoning from evidence.

clue.text: Repeat performance. from the choir

indicators.note: from shows the letters are taken out of the run of words the choir

explanation.surface: An encore given by the choir.
explanation.definitionFit: A reflected sound that repeats what was uttered, a natural reprise.

clue.text: Look out in this cave

parts.note: cave is not a hollow in rock but the classical word for beware, as in cave canem, so look out is said in that old tongue

explanation.surface: A warning to watch out while exploring a cavern.
explanation.walkthrough: Schoolboys shouted 'cave!' (beware) as a warning; it is the Latin imperative, 'look out'.
explanation.definitionFit: The language of ancient Rome, in which cave means beware.

clue.text: Course tackled again after second heat

definitions.text: Course tackled again after second heat

parts.words: Course tackled again after second heat
parts.note: reads like a race run again after another heat, but a dish served a second time after being warmed up

explanation.surface: Runners attempt the course again after the second heat of a race.
explanation.definitionFit: A warmed-over dish of leftovers, from the French for reheated.

clue.text: Honour with mitre

parts.note: the word mitre is what you get from an arrangement, an order, of the letters of merit

explanation.surface: A distinction awarded along with a bishop's headgear.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as an instruction: put the letters of MERIT in a new order and they make MITRE.
explanation.definitionFit: A British award for distinguished service given personally by the monarch, limited to 24 members.
